title: QiT: Quantum-Inspired Transformer for Visual Recognition Task
authors: Badri N. Patro, Vijay Agneeswaran
abstract: Quantum machine learning offers a compelling representational perspective: angle-encoded states inhabit Hilbert spaces in which periodic similarities and interactions can be expressed naturally. Realizing this perspective for visual recognition remains difficult, however, because present quantum neural networks are constrained by limited qubit counts, costly circuit simulation and measurement, noise, and unstable optimization on noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices. We investigate whether useful structural ideas from quantum models can instead be realized as scalable classical Transformer operations. We introduce QiT, a Quantum-inspired Transformer for vision tasks with three components: (i) angle-inspired encoding that maps image tokens to learned trigonometric Hilbert-space features analogous to quantum rotation-based state encoding; (ii) self-attention over these periodic features, inducing a classical cosine kernel approximated to quantum fidelity kernels; and (iii) gated multiplicative emulation, a trainable classical surrogate for interaction terms found in variational circuits. All components are differentiable tensor operations, so QiT claims neither quantum computation nor quantum speedup and retains the $\mathcal{O}(N^2D)$ attention complexity of a standard Vision Transformer. Across image-classification benchmarks, QiT is competitive with a matched classical Transformer while avoiding the severe runtime cost observed for a small simulated quantum Transformer. QiT-B reaches 78.3\% ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy with 45.7M parameters and 11.5 GFLOPs. These results position QiT as a scalable baseline for isolating and evaluating quantum-motivated inductive biases in visual recognition.

infographic.key_insight: QiT shows that quantum-inspired angle encoding, cosine-style attention, and multiplicative gating can be implemented as a scalable classical Transformer for vision, without running a quantum circuit.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a practical baseline for testing quantum-motivated inductive biases in image recognition while keeping standard Transformer complexity and hardware requirements.
method: Angle-inspired token encoding uses trigonometric features analogous to rotation-based quantum state preparation.
Self-attention operates on periodic features to approximate a cosine/fidelity kernel.
Gated multiplicative blocks emulate interaction terms seen in variational quantum circuits.
infographic.evidence_signal: On image-classification benchmarks, QiT is competitive with a matched classical Transformer and QiT-B reports 78.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K with 45.7M parameters and 11.5 GFLOPs.
infographic.watch_item: The approach is not quantum and does not claim quantum speedup, so any gains should be interpreted as classical inductive-bias effects rather than evidence of quantum advantage.
infographic.paper_title: QiT: Quantum-Inspired Transformer for Visual Recognition Task

title: Learning to Program Adaptive Non-Local Observables for Machine Learning
authors: Yu-Ting Lee, Samuel Yen-Chi Chen, Huan-Hsin Tseng
abstract: Quantum neural networks (QNNs) are typically built from variational quantum circuits (VQCs), which are limited by local measurements. Adaptive non-local observables (ANO) address this by jointly optimizing circuit parameters and multi-qubit measurements. However, existing ANO-based VQCs learn only a single static observable that remains invariant across all inputs. We propose QFWP-ANO, a novel architecture which employs a classical hypernetwork to dynamically program VQC parameters and/or non-local observables conditioned on each input. On multivariate time-series forecasting across four ETT datasets, QFWP-ANO achieves the lowest MSE in 16 of 20 settings and second-lowest in the remaining four, surpassing ANO-based and other strong baselines. On reinforcement learning tasks, QFWP-ANO consistently surpasses ANO-VQCs. Our results establish input-conditioned ANO as an effective approach for enhancing QNNs.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that conditioning variational quantum circuits on each input via a classical hypernetwork can make adaptive non-local observables more effective than using a single fixed observable.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Input-conditioned ANO could improve quantum machine learning systems for forecasting and control tasks by increasing expressivity without changing the underlying quantum hardware.
method: Uses a classical hypernetwork to program VQC parameters and/or non-local observables from the current input.
Extends adaptive non-local observables from a single static measurement to input-dependent measurement and circuit adaptation.
Targets multivariate time-series forecasting and reinforcement learning as evaluation settings.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four ETT time-series datasets, QFWP-ANO achieved the lowest MSE in 16 of 20 settings and second-lowest in the other four, and it also outperformed ANO-VQCs on reinforcement learning tasks.
infographic.watch_item: The added classical conditioning and joint optimization may increase training complexity and implementation overhead, especially when scaling to larger quantum models.
infographic.paper_title: Learning to Program Adaptive Non-Local Observables for Machine Learning

title: Transformers as Intrinsic Optimizers for Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
authors: Kuan-Cheng Chen, Xiaotian Xu, Hiromichi Matsuyama, Wei-Hao Huang, Haomu Yuan, Yu Yamashiro
abstract: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a leading variational framework for combinatorial optimization on noisy intermediate-scale quantum hardware, but its practical performance depends strongly on the classical optimizer used to train its variational parameters. This outer-loop optimization is often nonconvex, initialization-sensitive, and costly when repeated across large families of related problem instances. In this work, we propose a Transformer-based intrinsic optimization framework for QAOA, in which the optimizer itself is learned and embedded directly into the hybrid quantum-classical loop. The proposed graph-conditioned Transformer processes problem structure, current QAOA parameters, measurement feedback, and recent optimization history to predict the next variational-parameter update, thereby reformulating instance-wise classical optimization as an amortized learned policy. We develop a mathematical formulation of this intrinsic-optimization perspective and evaluate the method on QAOA-based MaxCut benchmarks across multiple problem settings, with comparisons against representative classical and learned optimization baselines. The results demonstrate that Transformer-based intrinsic optimization can provide a structured and transferable mechanism for improving the classical component of hybrid quantum optimization algorithms.

infographic.key_insight: The paper turns QAOA’s classical optimizer into a learned Transformer policy that uses problem structure and optimization history to predict the next parameter update.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This can reduce repeated hand-tuned outer-loop optimization for families of similar quantum optimization instances, making QAOA training more scalable and transferable.
method: Graph-conditioned Transformer ingests the problem graph, current QAOA parameters, measurement feedback, and recent update history.
Learns an intrinsic optimization policy that outputs the next variational-parameter update instead of relying on a fixed classical optimizer.
Evaluated as an amortized optimizer for QAOA on MaxCut benchmarks across multiple problem settings.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports comparisons against representative classical and learned baselines on QAOA-based MaxCut benchmarks across multiple problem settings.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on how well the learned optimizer generalizes to unseen graphs, hardware noise, and deeper QAOA circuits.
infographic.paper_title: Transformers as Intrinsic Optimizers for Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm

title: Quantum Compiler Design for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
authors: Chenghong Zhu, Jiahan Chen, Keming He, Hongshun Yao, Zhaohui Yang, Jin-Guo Liu
abstract: Scalable quantum computation is expected to rely on fault-tolerant quantum computation (FTQC), in which quantum error correction (QEC) suppresses physical errors sufficiently to support reliable logical operations. This requires quantum compilation to move beyond general-purpose circuit optimization toward encoding-aware and protocol-structured compilation across the full stack of fault-tolerant quantum computers. Beyond circuit synthesis and hardware mapping, an FTQC compiler must lower algorithm-level operations into the logical gate set supported by the chosen code, coordinate encoded data and ancilla resources, realize logical operations together with repeated syndrome extraction under hardware constraints, and provide the resulting measurement stream to real-time decoding. This survey presents a full-stack view of compiler design for QEC-protected quantum computation. We organize existing work into three interacting layers: logical-level QEC compilation, physical-level QEC realization, and decoder runtime integration. At the logical level, we review surface-code lattice-surgery compilers, beyond-surface-code code-surgery frameworks including emerging qLDPC approaches, and compilation support for non-Clifford operations such as magic-state distillation and code switching. At the physical level, we survey hardware-aware QEC realization on superconducting, trapped-ion, and neutral-atom platforms. We further examine decoder models, real-time decoding systems, and frame-management mechanisms that close the feedback loop during fault-tolerant execution. Finally, we identify open challenges in cross-layer optimization, qLDPC compilation, compiler-decoder co-design, runtime adaptivity, and the development of integrated and benchmarkable FTQC compilation stacks. An actively maintained paper list is available at: github.com/chenghongz/QEC-compiler-design.

infographic.key_insight: Fault-tolerant quantum compilers must become code-aware, hardware-aware, and decoder-aware so they can translate algorithms into reliable logical operations under QEC constraints.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This survey frames compiler design as a full-stack systems problem that directly affects whether practical fault-tolerant quantum computers can execute scalable workloads on real hardware.
method: Organizes FTQC compilation into three layers: logical-level QEC compilation, physical-level QEC realization, and decoder runtime integration.
Reviews surface-code lattice surgery, beyond-surface-code and qLDPC code-surgery ideas, plus non-Clifford support via magic-state distillation and code switching.
Covers hardware-specific realization for superconducting, trapped-ion, and neutral-atom platforms, along with real-time decoding and frame management.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper is a survey of existing work and synthesizes cross-layer compiler, hardware, and decoder designs rather than reporting new benchmark results in the abstract.
infographic.watch_item: A key implementation risk is that qLDPC compilation and compiler-decoder co-design remain immature, so end-to-end stacks may be difficult to integrate and benchmark consistently.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Compiler Design for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing

title: Noise-Robust Quantum State Characterization for Remote State Preparation with Deep Learning
authors: Bo Tang, Zixuan Liao, Hao Li, Yilin Yang, Jiani Lei, Zengya Li
abstract: Quantum communication underpins secure information processing and scalable quantum networks. In particular, remote state preparation (RSP) enables efficient quantum state transfer, but accurately estimating target states under complex noise remains challenging. Here, we propose a Transformer-based Quantum State Characterizer (TQSC) model for noisy RSP experiments. Our model reconstructs experimentally prepared pure and mixed photonic polarization states from noisy measurements in complex scattering environments, while its attention patterns provide physically grounded insights into correlations among the measured observables. The method achieves a mean estimator-target fidelity exceeding 99.999% under complex scattering and dynamic Gaussian noise, while its robustness and generalization are further examined using Qiskit-simulated Bloch-ball states.Furthermore, in a practical MNIST image transmission task with held-out states, the decoded bit error rate is reduced from 50.34% to zero after TQSC post-processing. The TQSC model enables accurate tomographic characterization under dynamic noise and provides physically grounded post-hoc insights, holding promise for intelligent quantum information processing applications.

infographic.key_insight: A Transformer-based quantum state characterizer can reconstruct noisy remote-prepared quantum states with extremely high fidelity while revealing physically meaningful measurement correlations through attention patterns.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical path to robust quantum state tomography and post-processing for quantum communication systems operating under complex, dynamic noise.
method: Transformer-based Quantum State Characterizer (TQSC) for noisy RSP measurements
Reconstructs experimentally prepared pure and mixed photonic polarization states
Uses attention maps to interpret correlations among observables
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports mean estimator-target fidelity above 99.999% under complex scattering and dynamic Gaussian noise, with MNIST transmission bit error rate reduced from 50.34% to zero after TQSC post-processing.
infographic.watch_item: Results are promising, but deployment will need validation across broader hardware platforms, noise regimes, and real-time experimental constraints beyond the reported settings.
infographic.paper_title: Noise-Robust Quantum State Characterization for Remote State Preparation with Deep Learning

title: Beyond Hardware: Adaptive Algorithmic Control by State-Proxy Equalization
authors: Jianlong Lu, Hongrui Zhang, Vishal Sharathchandra Bajpe, Thorsten Koch, Ying Chen
abstract: Recent advances in quantum computing have been driven primarily by improvements in hardware. Here we show that substantial gains can instead arise from how finite computational resources are allocated throughout a quantum computation. We introduce Adaptive Algorithmic Control (A2C), a software paradigm founded on a State-Proxy Equalization theorem, which proves that the optimal allocation for a state-derived proxy-error functional equalizes cumulative computational hardness rather than physical time. The required computational hardness is inferred directly from the evolving quantum state, avoiding explicit reconstruction of the exponentially large many-body spectrum. Across quantum optimization problems containing up to 156 qubits, combining exact simulations, large-scale supercomputer computations and IBM quantum hardware experiments, A2C improves the low-energy sampling probabilities by $22\%$ to over $100,000\%$ under matched circuit depths and measurement budgets. These results demonstrate that quantum computational performance depends not only on hardware capabilities, but also on how finite computational resources are organized, establishing adaptive algorithmic control as a complementary software pathway for advancing quantum computation.

infographic.key_insight: Adaptive Algorithmic Control (A2C) reallocates finite quantum-computing resources based on a state-derived proxy for hardness, yielding better performance than hardware-only improvements.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a software-level control strategy for quantum simulations and optimization that can boost low-energy sampling without increasing circuit depth or measurement budget.
method: State-Proxy Equalization theorem guides optimal allocation of computational effort.
Infer cumulative hardness directly from the evolving quantum state instead of reconstructing the full many-body spectrum.
Adapt resource distribution during execution to match hardness rather than physical time.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across exact simulations, supercomputer runs, and IBM hardware tests on optimization problems up to 156 qubits, A2C improved low-energy sampling probabilities by 22% to over 100,000% under matched circuit depths and measurement budgets.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on accurate state-derived hardness estimation, which may be difficult to maintain for noisy systems or when state information is limited.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Hardware: Adaptive Algorithmic Control by State-Proxy Equalization

title: State-Space-Based FIR Filtering on a Quantum Computer
authors: Roope Salmi, Davide Rocchesso, Vesa Välimäki
abstract: Many signal processing tasks require intensive computations. Quantum computing promises to accelerate certain tasks, but algorithms must be designed around the limitations of quantum mechanics. This paper provides a quantum implementation of finite impulse response (FIR) filters, which are a widely used tool in classical signal processing. The filter can be parallelized and composed as part of larger quantum algorithms, with potential for speedups using quantum amplitude estimation and future fault-tolerant quantum hardware. To accomplish these properties, we introduce a state-space framework wherein sample-based signal processing is performed with unitary quantum circuits. We present the quantum delay gate as the quantum analog of the delay line in discrete-time signal processing. Unitary circuits intrinsically describe lossless systems, but we also implement lowpass and other bounded filters by emulating a projection operator. The FIR filter implementation is tested and demonstrated with a quantum circuit simulator.

infographic.key_insight: The paper maps FIR filtering into a unitary state-space quantum circuit, introducing a quantum delay gate to enable sample-based signal processing on a quantum computer.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a reusable building block for quantum signal processing pipelines, with potential future speedups when combined with amplitude estimation and fault-tolerant hardware.
method: Formulate FIR filtering in a state-space representation compatible with unitary quantum circuits.
Implement a quantum delay gate as the discrete-time delay-line analog.
Approximate bounded filters, such as lowpass behavior, via a projection-operator emulation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The approach was implemented and demonstrated using a quantum circuit simulator, validating the circuit design at the proof-of-concept level.
infographic.watch_item: Because the construction is unitary, it is naturally suited to lossless systems and may require careful approximation or emulation for general dissipative filters.
infographic.paper_title: State-Space-Based FIR Filtering on a Quantum Computer

title: A Case Study on Noise Resilient Operator Selection in Adaptive Variational Quantum Algorithms
authors: Soorya Haravu, Mafalda Ramôa, Bharath Sambasivam
abstract: Hardware noise has been shown to significantly impact the accuracy of ADAPT-VQE, a ground state preparation algorithm. While previous work has studied the impact of noise on its parameter optimization step, its impact on the critical operator selection step remains comparatively unexplored. In this work, we examine the impact of a variety of noise channels on this step, using a linear H$_3$ molecule as a test case. We show that, despite the selection criterion's natural resilience to some noise, both coherent and incoherent noise can prevent convergence for sufficiently high noise rates. We employ quantum error mitigation techniques--dynamical decoupling, zero noise extrapolation, and Pauli twirling--and show that when combined appropriately, these techniques are capable of restoring a successful convergence profile. Our results highlight how error mitigation can improve the performance of ADAPT-VQE and enable convergence in the presence of hardware noise, offering valuable insights into the implementation of the algorithm on near-term quantum hardware.

infographic.key_insight: Noise can disrupt the ADAPT-VQE operator selection step, but combining mitigation methods can restore convergence on a noisy quantum device.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For near-term quantum hardware, this shows that error-mitigation strategy selection is as important as ansatz design for making adaptive quantum algorithms work reliably.
method: Tested ADAPT-VQE operator selection on linear H3 under multiple coherent and incoherent noise channels.
Evaluated mitigation methods including dynamical decoupling, zero-noise extrapolation, and Pauli twirling.
Compared noise-only behavior against combined mitigation setups to assess convergence recovery.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using a linear H3 molecule as the benchmark, the abstract reports that sufficiently strong noise can block convergence, while appropriately combined mitigation techniques restore a successful convergence profile.
infographic.watch_item: The result is demonstrated on a small molecular case study, so performance and mitigation tuning may not transfer directly to larger chemistry problems or different hardware noise models.
infographic.paper_title: A Case Study on Noise Resilient Operator Selection in Adaptive Variational Quantum Algorithms

title: FT-Weave: Real-Time Compilation Framework for Reconfigurable Fault-Tolerant Quantum Architectures
authors: Wan-Hsuan Lin, Milan Kornjača, Chen Zhao, Sheng-Tao Wang, Jason Cong
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) is essential for large-scale quantum computation, but realizing useful application throughput requires coordinating resource preparation, assignment, routing, and logical execution under strict hardware and timing constraints. Many FTQC compilation approaches construct offline schedules using nominal or fixed magic-state factory throughput. Such schedules cannot respond to stochastic resource-preparation and teleportation outcomes, leading to execution stalls and hardware underutilization. In this work, we introduce FT-Weave, a stage-aware real-time FTQC compilation framework that jointly coordinates resource preparation, resource assignment, teleportation routing, and correction handling. By adapting to runtime resource availability and hardware constraints, FT-Weave allows preparation, communication, and logical execution to overlap. We instantiate FT-Weave on two representative neutral-atom, early FTQC architectures: transversal STAR and a T-state cultivation architecture. Under the evaluated hardware and latency model, FT-Weave achieves a speedup of up to 3X over a baseline compilation flow for simulations of the two-dimensional transverse-field Ising model. In the case study, we further find that maximizing exposed concurrency does not necessarily minimize execution time. Although fine-grained asynchronous execution can reduce local idle time, its smaller optimization windows and increased routing contention can outweigh these gains. Together, these results show that effective runtime coordination, rather then exposed parallelism alone, determines how efficiently FTQC resources translate into application throughput:FT-Weave provides a blueprint for solving this real-time orchestration problem across resource protocols and architectures.

infographic.key_insight: FT-Weave is a real-time, stage-aware FTQC compiler that coordinates preparation, routing, assignment, and corrections to keep fault-tolerant quantum workloads moving under stochastic hardware behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It shows that runtime orchestration, not just static parallelism, is critical for achieving high throughput on reconfigurable fault-tolerant quantum architectures.
method: Adapts scheduling to live resource availability instead of assuming fixed factory throughput.
Jointly manages resource preparation, teleportation routing, logical execution, and correction handling.
Targets two neutral-atom FTQC designs: transversal STAR and T-state cultivation.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the evaluated hardware and latency model, FT-Weave reached up to 3× speedup over a baseline compiler on two-dimensional transverse-field Ising model simulations.
infographic.watch_item: Fine-grained asynchrony can increase routing contention and shrink optimization windows, so more concurrency does not always translate into shorter execution time.
infographic.paper_title: FT-Weave: Real-Time Compilation Framework for Reconfigurable Fault-Tolerant Quantum Architectures

title: Quantum Graph Convolutional Networks: Implementation and Trainability Analysis
authors: Paul San Sebastian Sein, Theodor Iosif, Tilen G. Limbäck-Stokin, Kin Ian Lo, Yidong Liao
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) achieve state-of-the-art performance on graph-structured data, but training and inference on large graphs are often bottlenecked by memory constraints and sparse linear-algebra workloads. Quantum computing offers an alternative set of primitives that may improve scalability for graph learning. Building on the quantum graph neural network (QGNN) framework of Liao \textit{et al.}, this work implements two representative architectures --- the Simplified Graph Convolution (SGC) and Linear Graph Convolution (LGC) models --- and evaluates them on open benchmark graph datasets and semi-supervised learning tasks using quantum simulation. We compare predictive performance and optimization behavior against classical baselines, showing that the quantum models achieve competitive performance with fewer parameters. Finally, we present a cost gradient analysis that identifies the tasks for which the models showcased are trainable. This is followed by a classical simulability study to find regimes in which the proposed circuits remain robust during training.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that quantum implementations of simplified graph convolution models can match competitive graph-learning behavior while using fewer parameters, but trainability depends strongly on the task and circuit regime.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It suggests quantum graph neural networks could offer a resource-efficient alternative for graph analytics, while emphasizing the need to check optimization stability and simulability before deployment.
method: Implemented two QGNN variants: Simplified Graph Convolution (SGC) and Linear Graph Convolution (LGC).
Evaluated them on open benchmark graph datasets in semi-supervised learning settings using quantum simulation.
Analyzed cost gradients and classical simulability to assess trainability and robustness during training.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports comparisons against classical baselines on benchmark graph datasets, with performance and optimization behavior used to judge competitiveness and trainability.
infographic.watch_item: The results are based on quantum simulation, so practical hardware noise, scalability, and circuit depth may limit real-world performance.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Graph Convolutional Networks: Implementation and Trainability Analysis

title: Achieving the limits of automorphism gates
authors: Jin Ming Koh, Shayan Majidy, Aranya Chakraborty, Anqi Gong, Shi Jie Samuel Tan, Norman Y. Yao
abstract: Universal fault-tolerant quantum computing combines versatile but expensive operations with specialized but cheap ones. Its efficiency depends on how much computation can be pushed onto the cheap operations and on the size of the code needed to do so. Automorphism gates provide such cheap operations using only physical single-qubit Clifford gates and qubit permutations. Yet no general theory characterizes their maximum logical power or the minimum code size needed to attain it. We develop such a theory. For stabilizer codes encoding $k\geq3$ logical qubits, we show that the largest logical group attainable by automorphisms is generated by all addressable $S$ and $\mathrm{CX}$ gates, and we construct codes attaining it. While this group contains exponentially fewer gates than the full Clifford group, adding one suitable non-Clifford gate yields universality. We further classify the largest logical groups attainable using qubit permutations, physical single-qubit Cliffords, or both across general stabilizer and CSS codes, and derive refined bounds for self-dual CSS subclasses. Achieving the maximum-size logical group through automorphisms requires $n=Θ(2^k)$ physical qubits. By contrast, all addressable diagonal Clifford gates, generated by $S$ and $\mathrm{CZ}$, require only $n=Θ(k^2)$ physical qubits when implemented using physical single-qubit Cliffords alone. Both bounds are tight. This polynomial qubit cost extends beyond Cliffords to all addressable diagonal gates at any fixed level of the Clifford hierarchy, using physical single-qubit diagonal gates. Thus, for full addressability, the sharpest physical-qubit cost divide lies between diagonal and $\mathrm{CX}$-type gates, not between Clifford and non-Clifford gates.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proves tight limits on what logical gates can be realized cheaply by automorphism-based fault-tolerant codes, showing a sharp qubit-cost divide between diagonal gates and CX-type gates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives code designers a concrete target for minimizing physical-qubit overhead in fault-tolerant architectures while maximizing the logical gate set available from low-cost physical operations.
method: Characterize the largest logical gate groups achievable by automorphisms for stabilizer, CSS, and self-dual CSS codes.
Construct codes that attain the maximal group, including all addressable S and CX gates for k≥3 logical qubits.
Derive tight asymptotic qubit lower/upper bounds for realizing these groups and for broader diagonal gates at fixed Clifford-hierarchy levels.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports tight asymptotic results, including n=Θ(2^k) qubits for maximal automorphism gate groups and n=Θ(k^2) for addressable diagonal Clifford gates, with both bounds proven tight.
infographic.watch_item: The maximal CX-type logical group still requires exponentially many physical qubits, so implementations may be impractical for larger k despite the theoretical optimality.
infographic.paper_title: Achieving the limits of automorphism gates

title: Scalable logical qubits
authors: Matthias Troyer, Chetan Nayak, John Martinis
abstract: Utility-scale quantum computing will require executing long, complex algorithms with end-to-end error rates far below what physical qubits can support directly. Error-corrected logical qubits are needed to achieve this goal. To make the progress on logical qubits measurable and comparable we introduce the definition of scalable logical qubits: logical qubits preserved for long computations by repeated quantum error correction, capable of fault-tolerant universal operations with low-latency real-time decoding and feedback, and replicable to the hundreds or thousands, as required by applications. We characterize these scalable logical qubits along four coupled dimensions: reliability, scale, capability, and performance, and discuss trade-offs among these dimensions.

infographic.key_insight: The paper defines "scalable logical qubits" as error-corrected qubits that remain reliable over long computations and can support fault-tolerant universal operations at application scale.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a practical benchmark for tracking progress toward utility-scale quantum computing by tying logical-qubit performance to reliability, scale, capability, and low-latency decoding.
method: Defines scalable logical qubits using four coupled dimensions: reliability, scale, capability, and performance.
Frames the target in terms of repeated quantum error correction, real-time decoding, and feedback.
Highlights trade-offs among these dimensions to make progress measurable and comparable.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract is conceptual and definitional rather than reporting new experimental results; it emphasizes a framework for evaluation instead of a specific dataset or benchmark.
infographic.watch_item: Achieving scalable logical qubits depends on low-latency real-time decoding and feedback, which may become a major systems bottleneck at large scale.
infographic.paper_title: Scalable logical qubits

title: VQE Validation on the Mononuclear T1 (Blue-Copper) Site: A Stepping Stone to the Multi-Copper Laccase Cluster
authors: Lucia Malickova
abstract: Validating variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) pipelines on realistic chemical systems is a critical stepping stone toward tackling classically intractable molecules. In this work, we report emulator-based validation of the VQE workflow proposed for the copper active site, executed on the LRZ Eviden Qaptiva emulator. A problem-tailored ADAPT-VQE with a full singles-doubles-triples (S+D+T) pool removes over 99% of the correlation error, reaching a stable plateau at 4.03 mEh relative to exact diagonalisation (148 selected operators). This establishes a >40x improvement over the hardware-efficient ansatz (HEA). Finally, we frame these emulator results as a robust baseline for upcoming physical quantum hardware runs on Euro-Q-Exa.

infographic.key_insight: The study shows that a problem-tailored ADAPT-VQE with a full singles-doubles-triples operator pool can accurately validate a copper-site quantum chemistry workflow, cutting correlation error by over 99%.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical emulator baseline for preparing and benchmarking future quantum hardware runs on realistic transition-metal active sites such as the blue-copper center and, ultimately, laccase clusters.
method: Ran a VQE workflow on the LRZ Eviden Qaptiva emulator for the mononuclear T1 blue-copper site.
Used ADAPT-VQE with a full S+D+T operator pool to iteratively build the ansatz.
Compared results against exact diagonalisation and a hardware-efficient ansatz (HEA).
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a stable energy plateau at 4.03 mEh above exact diagonalisation after selecting 148 operators, with more than 40× improvement over HEA.
infographic.watch_item: The results are emulator-based, so performance on physical quantum hardware may differ due to noise, connectivity, and compilation overhead.
infographic.paper_title: VQE Validation on the Mononuclear T1 (Blue-Copper) Site: A Stepping Stone to the Multi-Copper Laccase Cluster

title: Experimental certification of the nonlocal advantages of quantum imaginarity
authors: Jian-Hao Wu, Kai-Yu Yuan, Yun-Xiang Tian, Hao-Ran Tan, Yan-Xin Rong, Zhen Shang
abstract: Quantum imaginarity is a distinct resource in quantum information theory, yet its nonlocal properties have not been fully explored. Here, we report an experimental study of the nonlocal advantage of quantum imaginarity (NAQI), in which local measurements on one subsystem can steer the average imaginarity of the conditional states of the other subsystem beyond the corresponding classical bound. The $l_1$-norm of imaginarity inequality is adopted as an experimentally accessible witness. A hybrid optimization algorithm that combines a genetic algorithm with sequential quadratic programming is developed to avoid local optima and accelerate the search for optimal measurement settings. Using polarization-encoded photonic qubits, we prepare two classes of two-qubit Bell-diagonal states and experimentally characterize the imaginarity of the conditional states following local measurements. Clear violations of the $l_1$-norm of imaginarity inequality are observed, providing an experimental certification of NAQI. We further investigate the relationship among NAQI, the nonlocal advantage of quantum coherence (NAQC), and Bell nonlocality based on their respective inequality criteria. For the two-qubit Werner states considered in this work, the regions of states that violate the respective criteria satisfy $\mathcal{D}_{\rm NAQC}\subset\mathcal{D}_{\rm NAQI}\subset\mathcal{D}_{\rm BN}$. Our work provides an experimental realization of NAQI and a comparison of different forms of quantum nonclassicality in a photonic platform.

infographic.key_insight: The paper experimentally demonstrates nonlocal advantage of quantum imaginarity (NAQI): local measurements can steer a partner qubit into conditional states with imaginarity exceeding the classical bound.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a measurable new nonclassical resource and a practical benchmark for quantum photonic control, state characterization, and resource-based quantum protocol design.
method: Prepared polarization-encoded two-qubit Bell-diagonal states in a photonic experiment.
Used the l1-norm of imaginarity inequality as the operational witness for NAQI.
Applied a hybrid genetic algorithm + sequential quadratic programming method to optimize measurement settings and avoid local optima.
infographic.evidence_signal: The experiment reported clear violations of the l1-norm imaginarity inequality for two classes of two-qubit states, and mapped the state regions showing \(\mathcal{D}_{\rm NAQC}\subset\mathcal{D}_{\rm NAQI}\subset\mathcal{D}_{\rm BN}\) for Werner states.
infographic.watch_item: The result depends on experimentally prepared Bell-diagonal photonic states and inequality-based witnesses, so performance and generality may vary with noise, state family, and measurement optimization quality.
infographic.paper_title: Experimental certification of the nonlocal advantages of quantum imaginarity

title: Lazy training of quantum physics informed neural networks
authors: Anderson Melchor Hernandez, Giacomo De Palma
abstract: We study the gradient-flow training dynamics of quantum physics-informed neural networks (QPINNs) for the solution of second-order elliptic partial differential equations with Dirichlet boundary conditions. We consider parameterized quantum circuits as function approximators and analyze their overparameterized regime through the lens of the neural tangent kernel (NTK). Our contribution is a nonasymptotic lazy-training theory for QPINNs and their variational formulation: we prove that, for sufficiently large circuit width, the nonlinear gradient flow is quantitatively approximated by a linearized NTK model, with explicit bounds depending on the number of qubits, circuit depth, circuit light-cone geometry, and the dimension of the domain of the solution to the PDE.

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that sufficiently wide quantum physics-informed neural networks (QPINNs) can be trained in a lazy regime where the nonlinear gradient flow is accurately captured by a linearized neural tangent kernel (NTK) model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a quantitative theory for when quantum circuit-based PDE solvers can be expected to train predictably, with bounds tied to qubit count, depth, light-cone geometry, and domain dimension.
method: Analyze gradient-flow training dynamics of QPINNs for second-order elliptic PDEs with Dirichlet boundary conditions.
Use overparameterized NTK theory to derive a nonasymptotic lazy-training approximation for parameterized quantum circuits.
Prove explicit approximation bounds for both the nonlinear model and its variational formulation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a theoretical, nonasymptotic analysis rather than experiments, with guarantees expressed through explicit bounds on approximation error under sufficient circuit width.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees rely on large-width, overparameterized circuits, so practical performance may degrade for smaller or hardware-constrained quantum models.
infographic.paper_title: Lazy training of quantum physics informed neural networks

title: Quantum Simulation of Dissipative Non-Markovian Coupled Classical Oscillators
authors: Malte Schade, Sophia Simon, Nathan Wiebe, Scott Keating, Cyrill Bösch, Andreas Fichtner
abstract: We present a quantum algorithm for simulating classical oscillator networks characterized by non-Markovian dissipation and time-varying material properties, extending recent speedups for undamped harmonic systems to viscoacoustic and viscoelastic media. We embed the history-dependent dynamics into a Markovian state space governed by a non-Hermitian operator by approximating memory kernels through a Prony series. We then use linear combination of Hamiltonian simulation to estimate the instantaneous kinetic and potential energy for a subset of oscillators at time $t$ within error $ε$ using a number of queries to the oscillator system that scales as $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(α_{\rm tot} t/ε)$, where $α_{\rm tot}$ is polynomial in the strength of the dissipation, spring constants, inverse masses, and sparsity of the connections in the network. We further show that this energy estimation task is in the worst-case classically hard (i.e., a corresponding decision problem is $\mathsf{BQP}$-complete), even in the presence of strong dissipation. For time-dependent materials, we show that changes in material properties appear as effective dissipation or growth in the energy representation. Additionally, we prove the infeasibility of exponential quantum advantages in locally coupled topologies through a novel form of Lieb-Robinson-like bounds that apply to differential equations. This allows our quantum algorithms to provide quartic speedups for locally coupled damped oscillator systems in three dimensions, raising the possibility of practical quantum speedups for realistically damped oscillator networks and approximated wave equations.

infographic.key_insight: A quantum algorithm simulates dissipative, non-Markovian coupled oscillator networks by converting memory effects into a Markovian form and estimating local energy efficiently.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This could accelerate simulation of viscoacoustic and viscoelastic systems, with implications for wave propagation modeling, materials with time-varying properties, and damped mechanical networks.
method: Approximate memory kernels with a Prony series to embed history-dependent dynamics into a Markovian state space.
Use linear-combination-of-Hamiltonian-simulation techniques on a non-Hermitian operator representation.
Estimate instantaneous kinetic and potential energy for selected oscillators with query complexity scaling as ~O(α_tot t/ε).
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports provable query-scaling speedups and a BQP-completeness result for the associated decision problem, including quartic gains for locally coupled damped systems in 3D.
infographic.watch_item: The approach relies on accurate kernel approximation and problem structure; practical performance may degrade if the Prony-series fit or sparsity assumptions are poor.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Simulation of Dissipative Non-Markovian Coupled Classical Oscillators

title: Improving Sample Efficiency in Peptide-HLA Binding Prediction with Hybrid Quantum-Classical Neural Networks
authors: Chenyan Jia, Cong Guo, Siyue Chen, Pengpeng Ye, Xiaochun Chen
abstract: Peptide-HLA binding prediction is a critical step in neoantigen identification for personalized cancer immunotherapy and holds significant clinical value. However, the training data available for many HLA alleles are extremely limited, which severely constrains the performance of conventional methods on this task. Parameterized quantum circuits are hypothesized to induce inductive biases beneficial for learning from small datasets, yet their application to biological sequence prediction remains underexplored. To address this, we propose a hybrid quantum-classical neural network (HQNN) specifically designed for peptide-HLA binding prediction. HQNN integrates multi-source biological feature encoding with parallel quantum feature extractors and a quantum-enhanced classifier. On two HLA alleles (A*02:01 and B*07:02), HQNN outperforms a parameter-matched classical CNN baseline across all training sizes, with the performance gap widening as training data decreases. Ablation studies confirm the respective contributions of the quantum feature extraction module and the quantum classifier. In noise-aware simulations, performance degrades only mildly, and such degradation is reasonable and acceptable under realistic quantum hardware noise levels. These results suggest that hybrid quantum-classical architectures can provide practical sample-efficiency gains for immunoinformatics tasks in low-data regimes.

infographic.key_insight: A hybrid quantum-classical neural network can improve sample efficiency for peptide-HLA binding prediction, especially when training data are scarce.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests quantum-enhanced models may be useful for low-data bioinformatics and immunotherapy pipelines where accurate prediction matters but labeled data are limited.
method: Multi-source biological features encode peptide-HLA inputs.
Parallel quantum feature extractors learn compact representations.
A quantum-enhanced classifier combines extracted signals for binding prediction.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across two HLA alleles (A*02:01 and B*07:02), HQNN beat a parameter-matched classical CNN at all training sizes, with larger gains in smaller-data settings; ablations and noise-aware simulations supported the design.
infographic.watch_item: The reported benefits come from simulation on only two alleles, so broader validation and hardware-scale testing are still needed.
infographic.paper_title: Improving Sample Efficiency in Peptide-HLA Binding Prediction with Hybrid Quantum-Classical Neural Networks

title: Securing quantum error correction against misleading advice from AI agents
authors: A. Barış Özgüler
abstract: Can an attacker turn influence over an artificial intelligence (AI) adviser into a harmful quantum error-correction update? We identify an ambiguity in passive syndrome records that obstructs recovery selection, then show how additional calibration measurements support certified recovery updates under uncertainty and drift. In an odd-distance square toric code with error-free preparation, syndrome measurements, and recovery operations, opposite coherent $X$ rotations produce identical passive syndrome-history distributions. Yet a fixed phase correction can help at one sign and harm at the other. A terminal logical measurement on known encoded calibration states supplies the missing sign information. A separate evaluator accepts an update only when calibration uncertainty and a justified drift bound certify improvement over the current recovery, without assuming that the adviser recommends correctly. In simulated advice attacks, calibration-confidence checks reject harmful proposals while retaining beneficial updates under honest advice. We derive sufficient limits on calibration age that require improvement through deployment. In matched simulations, a validated channel-specific bound retains more beneficial updates than the general bound after accounting for evaluation time, while preventing the tested harmful activations under the stated drift assumption. A separate surface-code experiment includes stochastic circuit faults and noise changing during acquisition. Deterministic controllers achieve at least as many beneficial updates with the same observations. Violating the drift assumption permits harmful acceptance in the toric experiment. The results identify information required for recovery selection, establish conditional guarantees against harmful updates, and quantify the recovery improvements forgone through conservative acceptance.

infographic.key_insight: Passive syndrome histories can be ambiguous, so safe quantum error-correction updates need extra calibration measurements and drift-aware certification before trusting AI advice.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For fault-tolerant quantum hardware, this work provides a practical decision rule to accept only recovery updates that are provably beneficial under uncertainty, reducing the risk of AI-driven harmful control changes.
method: Showed that opposite coherent X rotations can generate identical passive syndrome-history distributions in an odd-distance square toric code.
Used terminal logical measurements on known calibration states to recover the missing sign information needed for safe recovery selection.
Built an evaluator that accepts an update only when calibration confidence and a justified drift bound certify improvement over the current recovery.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations of advice attacks and noisy surface-code experiments showed that the certification checks rejected harmful proposals while retaining beneficial updates, with a validated channel-specific bound outperforming the general bound after accounting for evaluation time.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees depend on a drift assumption and calibration age limits; if noise drifts too much or those limits are violated, harmful acceptance can still occur.
infographic.paper_title: Securing quantum error correction against misleading advice from AI agents

title: Optical Quantum Computing
authors: Hamza Hasnaoui, Leonardo Limongi, Taira Giordani, Beatrice Polacchi, Alberto Quaranta, Martino Bernard
abstract: Under the label of optical quantum computing, there are a variety of protocols and experiments that use the quantum properties of light to achieve a computational advantage over classical computing machines. In this review, we describe some of the main implementations, which differ in the type of encoding and in how the computation is performed, whether using gates or cluster states. For each protocol, we describe advantages and challenges with an overview of the experimental results obtained, summarized in tables. Because of the great relevance achieved in this field, there is a section dedicated to non-universal quantum computation with photons, where boson sampling, variational quantum eigensolvers, and quantum machine learning applications are described. The aim is to give the reader the broadest overview of the applications where photons and their quantum properties play a key role in computation.

infographic.key_insight: Optical quantum computing uses photonic quantum states to realize both universal and non-universal computation, with multiple encoding and computation paradigms offering different tradeoffs in capability and practicality.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The review helps researchers and engineers compare photonic architectures, experimental maturity, and application fit when designing quantum computing systems for gates, cluster states, boson sampling, or quantum machine learning.
method: Surveyed major optical quantum computing implementations and their encoding strategies
Compared gate-based and cluster-state computation approaches
Summarized experimental results, advantages, and challenges across protocols, including non-universal photonic methods
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper is a review that synthesizes experimental results into tables rather than reporting a single benchmark, aiming to provide a broad overview of protocol performance and application areas.
infographic.watch_item: Photonic quantum computing remains implementation-dependent, with scalability, loss, and experimental complexity likely limiting near-term practical deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Optical Quantum Computing

title: Proof of a positive coherent-error threshold for topological quantum codes
authors: Shiro Tamiya, Masato Koashi
abstract: Threshold analyses of quantum error-correcting codes are well established for stochastic error models, in which errors occur randomly with given probabilities. However, errors in actual devices can also be coherent, such as unwanted $Z$ rotations due to imperfect control, which are not captured by stochastic error models. For the surface code, numerical studies have indicated threshold behavior even under coherent errors, but a rigorous proof of threshold existence is lacking. Here we prove that a positive threshold for coherent $Z$-rotation errors exists for quantum low-density parity-check codes with a bounded number of logical qubits, including the surface code and other topological codes. Specifically, we show that the maximum-likelihood Pauli recovery suppresses the entanglement infidelity exponentially in the code distance up to a prefactor linear in the number of physical qubits whenever the rotation angles lie below a constant that is independent of the code size. The proof combines Fourier analysis to retain the interference among the amplitudes of coherent errors with the cluster expansion of abstract polymer models. Our results expand the theoretical foundation of quantum error correction and offer a statistical-mechanical description of quantum error correction beyond stochastic errors.

infographic.key_insight: The paper rigorously proves that topological quantum codes can still exhibit a positive error threshold under coherent Z-rotation noise, with logical infidelity decaying exponentially with code distance below a size-independent angle limit.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This strengthens the theoretical case for using surface code and related topological LDPC codes in hardware where control errors are coherent rather than purely stochastic.
method: Uses Fourier analysis to preserve interference between coherent error amplitudes.
Applies cluster expansion of abstract polymer models to bound logical failure.
Analyzes maximum-likelihood Pauli recovery for bounded-logical-qubit topological codes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a rigorous threshold proof and an exponential suppression guarantee for entanglement infidelity under coherent rotation angles below a constant independent of code size.
infographic.watch_item: The result is proven for coherent Z-rotation errors and codes with a bounded number of logical qubits, so broader noise models and finite-precision decoder implementations may need separate validation.
infographic.paper_title: Proof of a positive coherent-error threshold for topological quantum codes
